explanations.explanation: This neuron detects sentence‐ or clause-level discourse markers—formulaic connective or hedging phrases (e.g. “in either case,” “or so,” “all too often,” “needless to say,” “on one hand,” “if so”) that frame, qualify or transition between statements.

This neuron detects the “dot” of abbreviations and initialisms—i.e. periods that belong to titles, initials, month or domain‐name abbreviations (F. Campbell, Oct., Nov., X. Zhou, .com, etc.) rather than true sentence-ending full stops.
This neuron fires on subword tokens that mark the start of a major name or brand component—e.g. the initial chunk of a person’s name, a company/ product title, or other proper‐noun segment.

This neuron fires whenever the model sees a content‐bearing subword (a root or semantically rich morpheme) – for example “meas-” in “measurement,” “mach-” in “machinery,” “nail-” in “nailing,” “ous” in “desirous,” “ent” in “enthroned,” as well as whole open-class words like “doors,” “eyes,” “snow,” “palms,” etc. It flags the core semantic pieces of content words.

This neuron consistently spikes on the very first subword of longer, semantically rich words—especially Latin‐derived roots in Romance and Germanic languages. In other words, it’s a “root-onset” detector: it marks the BPE prefix where a new content word (morpheme-carrying stem) begins.

This feature fires on concessive/exceptional discourse markers—words or phrases (e.g. “apart from,” “except for,” “aside from,” “as much as,” “on the other hand”) that introduce exceptions or contrasts.

This neuron lights up on sentence-initial discourse signals—connective adverbs or interjections (e.g. “Alternatively,” “Sure,” “Put…,” “Listen…”) that frame a shift in stance, introduce alternatives, or launch instructions.

This feature fires on specialised shorthand tokens—abbreviations and acronyms (e.g. measurement units like “kg,” “ft,” “sf,” organisation or concept initialisms like “PPP,” “JICA,” “NIHR,” “RLS,” and legal-boilerplate terms like “hereinafter”)—marking the presence (and often the end) of a compact multi-word label.

This feature detects the little “linking” words that head prepositional/particle attachments in English—prepositions and directional particles (with, at, to, on, of, about, behind, over, up to, etc.) that introduce and connect a phrase onto a verb or noun.

This neuron fires when the model sees a relatively rare, content‐bearing subword (a root or affix) – in practice odd little letter‐chunks like “erv,” “der,” “azed,” “ident,” “lect,” “ribut,” “put,” etc. – i.e. unusual BPE segments that typically mark semantic stems or morphological affixes.
This feature detects the numeric day‐of‐month token in full date expressions (e.g. the “28” in “August 28, 1997,” “22” in “Oct. 22, 2015,” etc.).

This neuron is essentially a “morpheme-stem” detector for Greek/Latin roots in technical vocabulary.  It lights up whenever you hit a subword that begins a familiar scientific or medical root (e.g. rif- in centrifuge, inos- in inositol, sil- in siloxy, spinal in cerebrospinal, fel- in Creutzfeldt, Cal- in Calmette, Heart in Heart Institute, etc.).

This neuron fires whenever the model sees the start of a capitalized subword inside a longer word—i.e. the “in-word” uppercase letter that begins a new piece of a multi-part proper name (McGuinness, Van Buren, OBASA, Jeremiah, etc.).

This neuron lights up on discourse markers of purpose, intention or obligation—words and constructions that state aims, reasons or responsibilities (e.g. “goal/aim,” “reason,” “need,” “cases,” or infinitives like “to deal,” “to cope,” “to provide”).

This neuron is essentially picking out the noun-head of a category or list item—especially those built with the “-er/-ers” or plural “-s” ending (e.g. placeholder, popovers, pullovers, needs, melodies)—marking when the text shifts into naming a page type, product or content category.

This neuron fires on the initial subword of proper‐name entities—especially place, region or organization names. It peaks on prefixes like “Nor” (Norwood, Nordea, Norwich), “Wat” (Watford), “Mal” (Maldives), “Or” (Orion), “Ever” (Everton/Goodison), etc., marking the beginnings of geographic or institutional names.

This feature appears to light up on the very “labels” or “headers” that kick off a new entry or section—whether it’s the words Beginning/Description or date‐and‐time tokens (years, ordinals, month–day stamps). In other words, it detects those front-of-entry markers that signal “here comes a new segment.”

This feature flags sentence-initial, capitalized tokens that serve as the lead word of a heading or FAQ-style question (e.g. “What,” “Don’t,” “Discover,” “According,” “Aims”), marking the start of a new section or title.
This feature fires on the launch of a direct quoted remark in sports‐news prose—i.e. the opening quotation mark (and first word) of a speaker’s reported speech following a “said”/attribution clause.
This feature fires whenever the model sees a full‐stop “.” token—i.e. end‐of‐sentence (or abbreviation) punctuation marking a boundary in the text.
